article.headline: One-Year Real Rates Near Zero Again — Is Another Melt-Up Coming?
article.lede: The one-year real rate — the nominal Treasury yield minus the market's expected inflation — has fallen to +0.31%, sitting only 30 basis points above zero. @Globalflows argues this proximity to negative territory echoes the conditions that produced the 2021 risk-asset melt-up, when deeply negative real rates pushed investors out of cash and into equities. Whether the historical analogy holds depends on a distinction the chart alone cannot make.
article.body:
**Real rates** — nominal Treasury yields minus the market's inflation expectation — have fallen to +0.31% at the one-year tenor, a level not seen since the Federal Reserve's zero-rate era. When the real rate turns negative, every dollar parked in cash quietly loses purchasing power, making any asset that offers positive real prospects relatively more attractive. At 30 basis points from that threshold, the signal @Globalflows is highlighting is not subtle.

The 2021 comparison has real substance. In late 2021, the one-year real rate bottomed at −4.46% — a product of CPI running at 7% while the Fed anchored the overnight rate near zero and purchased $120 billion of securities each month. The result was the *TINA* trade (“there is no alternative to equities”) at full intensity: the S&P 500 returned roughly 27%, the Nasdaq Composite rose 21%, and speculative assets — SPACs, meme stocks, early crypto — dramatically outperformed. With cash guaranteed to erode in real terms, capital had no choice but to move up the risk curve.

The bullish arithmetic is straightforward. Equity valuations are the present value of future earnings discounted at a real rate; when that rate falls, *discounted-cash-flow* denominators shrink and price-to-earnings multiples expand mechanically, without any improvement in underlying earnings. The S&P 500's forward earnings multiple sits at 21.0 times — above its five-year average of 19.9 and its ten-year average of 18.9 — suggesting some repricing has already occurred. First-quarter 2026 earnings growth for S&P 500 companies came in at 27.7%, the highest reading since Q4 2021, which provides additional fundamental support.

The critical question is what is doing the work. In 2021, real rates went negative because the Fed deliberately held nominal yields near zero while the economy reflated — a condition economists call *ZIRP*. Today, the nominal one-year Treasury sits near 3.8%. The arithmetic resolves to +0.31% real because one-year inflation expectations have risen to approximately 3.5%, driven by tariff-related supply shocks and energy prices, not by policy suppression of nominal yields. GDP growth came in at 0.7% in the first quarter of 2026. That combination — sticky inflation, weak growth, a Fed that cannot cut — is closer to the *stagflationary* template of the 1970s than to the zero-rate reflation of 2021. Ray Dalio warned as recently as April 2026 that the U.S. is “certainly in a stagflationary period.” International Monetary Fund research suggests that the link between low real rates and strong equity returns holds reliably at low-to-moderate inflation but turns unreliable once CPI materially exceeds 4%, precisely because inflation at that level signals supply-side dysfunction rather than policy accommodation.

None of this makes the thesis wrong. Markets are already at records — S&P 500 at 7,444 and the Nasdaq Composite at 26,402 as of May 12, 2026 — validating the broad direction. The question is whether those records persist if real rates cross zero for a reason the *melt-up* playbook did not anticipate.

concepts.definition: The nominal yield on a fixed-income security minus the expected inflation rate over the same period. A positive real rate means cash earns more than inflation erodes; a negative real rate means holding cash destroys purchasing power in inflation-adjusted terms, typically pushing investors toward assets with positive real return prospects.

Shorthand for the investment thesis that when safe assets such as cash or government bonds offer negative real returns, investors have no viable alternative but to hold equities or other risk assets. Repopularized during the zero-rate era of 2009–2022, it is used to explain persistent equity multiple expansion in low-rate environments.

A central bank strategy of holding the benchmark overnight rate at or near 0%, typically deployed during recessions or deflationary episodes to maximize monetary accommodation. The Federal Reserve operated under ZIRP from December 2008 to December 2015, and again from March 2020 to March 2022.

A simultaneous combination of stagnant economic growth and elevated inflation. It complicates monetary policy because rate cuts that might support growth would worsen inflation, while rate hikes that might control inflation risk deepening the slowdown. The paradigm case is the 1970s U.S. economy, when both unemployment and CPI rose together.

A valuation method that calculates the present value of an asset by estimating its future cash flows and dividing each by a factor reflecting the time value of money. When real discount rates fall, the present value of the same future cash flows rises mechanically — a key driver of equity multiple expansion during low-rate environments.

A rapid, self-reinforcing rise in asset prices driven more by investor fear of missing out and mechanical capital reallocation than by fundamental improvements in earnings or economic activity. The term contrasts with a melt-down; both imply momentum that outruns underlying fundamentals.

The ratio of a stock's or index's current price to its expected earnings per share over the next twelve months. A higher forward P/E means investors are paying more for each dollar of projected earnings, reflecting optimism about growth, a lower discount rate, or both.

article.fact_check: The 2021 analog is factually grounded — 1-year real rates did reach −4.46% in November of that year, per the Bloomberg chart. What the comparison elides is that in 2021 real rates were negative primarily because the Fed was suppressing nominal yields near zero. Today the same arithmetic produces a +0.31% real rate from elevated inflation expectations (~3.5%) meeting moderately elevated nominal yields (~3.8%), not from ZIRP. Whether that mechanistic difference changes the asset-price implications is genuinely debated, but the historical comparison is not a perfect like-for-like.
